---
title: "Quiz: filtered back-projection and sampling"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** What does the ramp filter do to the spectrum of a projection, and why is that the right correction?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think of the spokes of the Fourier slice theorem.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It multiplies the projection's 1D spectrum by $|\omega|$: low frequencies down, high ones up. Every projection contributes a spoke through the centre of the 2D spectrum, so the spokes crowd near the centre; weighting each spoke by its distance from the centre (in proportion to the gap it must cover) gives every frequency its fair share. It undoes the $1/|\omega|$ of plain back-projection.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why does the filtered projection of a point have negative values, and what are they for?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A ramp suppresses the low frequencies, so the filtered profile has zero (or almost zero) total and must dip below zero beside the peak. Back-projected, the negative dips form dark bands along each smear; around the point they cancel the positive tails of the smears from other angles, which removes the $1/r$ halo.
:::

---

**Q3.** A reconstruction from a low-dose scan is grainy. Which filter would you choose instead of the ramp, and what do you lose?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where is the noise in frequency?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A tapered ramp (Hann, cosine, or Shepp–Logan), possibly with a lower cutoff. The noise sits mostly at high frequencies, which the ramp amplifies most; the taper turns them down. The price is resolution: edges and small details blur.
:::

---

**Q4.** Your projections have 256 bins. Roughly how many angles over 180° should you acquire? What happens with 60?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
About $\tfrac{\pi}{2}\cdot 256 \approx 400$. With 60 the spokes far from the centre of the spectrum are much more than one frequency step apart: streaks radiate from high-contrast edges.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why must each projection be zero-padded before filtering it with an FFT?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Multiplying DFTs is **circular** convolution: the kernel's tail that sticks out at one end of the projection reappears at the other end. Padding with zeros to at least twice the length gives the tail room, so the result equals ordinary (linear) convolution. Without padding, values near the edges of the object are wrong (for a large object: darker towards its rim).
:::

---

**Q6.** An electron tomography tilt series covers $\pm 65°$. What is missing from the data, and how does a round particle look in the reconstruction?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A wedge of $180° - 130° = 50°$ around the beam direction in the 2D spectrum is never measured. The particle is elongated along the beam direction and its edges facing the beam are blurred: it looks like a lemon. No filter can restore the missing frequencies; only prior knowledge can partly fill them in.
:::

---

**Q7.** With a fixed number of photons for the whole scan, why is it usually better to take many noisy views than a few clean ones with FBP?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The noise in the reconstruction depends mostly on the total number of photons, however they are shared. Too few views add a different error, streaks from missing spokes, that more photons per view cannot fix. Spreading the dose avoids the streaks at little cost in noise.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Where does the $|\omega|$ in FBP come from mathematically?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
From the Jacobian of polar coordinates: writing the 2D inverse Fourier transform with $\boldsymbol\omega = \omega\,\mathbf n_\theta$ gives $d\boldsymbol\omega = |\omega|\,d\omega\,d\theta$. With the slice theorem the inner integral becomes the inverse 1D transform of $|\omega|P_\theta(\omega)$, and the outer integral over $\theta$ is back-projection.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* The noise variance of FBP scales as $\omega_c^3$. By how much does the noise standard deviation grow if the cutoff is raised from 0.25 to 0.5 cycles per pixel?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Variance $\times 2^3 = 8$, standard deviation $\times\sqrt8 \approx 2.8$.
:::
